wages.amount_text: Wages, salaries and commissions are fully exempt from attachment while in the employer's hands, except for support, divorce, board of four weeks or less, residential-lease judgments (capped at 10% of net wages), PHEAA student loans, and criminal restitution/fines/costs

retirement.amount_text: $1,000,000 plus income and distributions from employee benefit plans (ERISA plans and IRC 401, 403, 408, 408A, 409, 414, 457, 501(a) arrangements)
retirement.notes: ERISA-qualified plans are excluded from the estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds regardless of state law. State cite: § 43-45-16 lets a person 'select and designate a total of one million dollars and the income and distributions therefrom from the employee's benefit plans as exempt', subject to the State's and its subdivisions' right to collect amounts owed to them and to qualified domestic relations orders. § 43-45-17 defines employee benefit plan (ERISA plans and IRC §§ 401, 403(a), 403(b), 408, 408A, 409, 414, 457, 501(a) arrangements). The state cap matters only where the federal provisions do not reach.

south-dakota.research_notes: All seven categories quoted from sdlegislature.gov (its /api/Statutes/<section>.html endpoint serves the official text; the main site is a JavaScript app). Opt-out state. Homestead is flagged only because the $170,000 age-70 sentence in § 43-45-3 is ambiguously placed and was amended by SL 2025, ch 185, which was not read; the unlimited-value rule and acreage limits themselves are clear. No vehicle or tools exemption: both come out of the $7,000 (head of family) / $5,000 wildcard. Wage garnishment limit (20%, 40x minimum wage) is more protective than the federal CCPA. Bankruptcy court (sdb.uscourts.gov) not consulted.

tennessee.doubling_note: Homestead: individuals who jointly own and use a principal residence share a combined cap of $52,500, divided equally when both claim in the same proceeding (§ 26-2-301(a)(1)), so it does not fully double; the § 26-2-103 personal-property exemption is per 'person' and the statute is silent on joint filers (secondary source).
tennessee.effective_date_note: Per the FindLaw annotation, 2021 Pub. Acts c. 301, § 2 (eff. January 1, 2022) deleted former § 26-2-301(e) and (f); the current $35,000 / $52,500 homestead text is presumed to date from that act, but the public chapter itself could not be fetched (publications.tnsosfiles.com returned 403). No CPI indexing.

homestead.amount_text: $35,000 per individual; $52,500 combined for joint owners who both claim
homestead.notes: 'An individual, whether a head of family or not, shall be entitled to a homestead exemption upon real property which is owned by the individual and used by the individual or the individual's spouse or dependent, as a principal place of residence. The aggregate value of such homestead exemption shall not exceed thirty-five thousand dollars ($35,000); provided, individuals who jointly own and use real property as their principal place of residence shall be entitled to homestead exemptions, the aggregate value of which exemptions combined shall not exceed fifty-two thousand five hundred dollars ($52,500), which shall be divided equally among them'. Does not operate against public taxes, purchase-money or improvement debts, or debts secured by a written waiver (§ 26-2-301(c)). Former (e)-(f) (other tiers) deleted by 2021 Pub. Acts c. 301, eff. 1/1/2022. Source is FindLaw's copy of the Tennessee Code, marked 'last updated January 02, 2024'; no primary text was reachable, so later amendments would not show.

motor_vehicle.amount_text: No vehicle-specific exemption located; vehicle equity is claimed within the $10,000 personal-property exemption (secondary source)
motor_vehicle.notes: Sections 26-2-102 to 26-2-112 as read on FindLaw contain no vehicle-specific exemption; § 26-2-103 lets the debtor select any owned personal property up to $10,000 of equity. Not confirmed against a primary source or a court exemption sheet, so not recorded as 'None'. Source is FindLaw's copy of the Tennessee Code, marked 'last updated January 02, 2024'; no primary text was reachable, so later amendments would not show.

household_goods.amount_text: No separate dollar cap: necessary wearing apparel, family portraits and pictures, family Bible and school books exempt; other household goods within the $10,000 personal-property exemption
household_goods.notes: § 26-2-104(a): in addition to § 26-2-105, exempt articles include (1) all necessary and proper wearing apparel of the debtor and family and their receptacles, (2) all family portraits and pictures, (3) the family Bible and school books (remaining items of (a) not read this pass). Other household goods fall within the § 26-2-103 $10,000 aggregate. Source is FindLaw's copy of the Tennessee Code, marked 'last updated January 02, 2024'; no primary text was reachable, so later amendments would not show.

wildcard.amount_text: $10,000 aggregate equity in any personal property, including cash and bank deposits
wildcard.notes: 'Personal property to the aggregate value of ten thousand dollars ($10,000) debtor's equity interest shall be exempt ... Such person may select for exemption the items of the owned and possessed personal property, including money and funds on deposit with a bank or other financial institution'. Property bought or maintained with fraudulently obtained funds is ineligible (§ 26-2-103(b)). Source is FindLaw's copy of the Tennessee Code, marked 'last updated January 02, 2024'; no primary text was reachable, so later amendments would not show.

wages.amount_text: Garnishment capped at the lesser of 25% of weekly disposable earnings or the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 30 x the federal minimum hourly wage
wages.notes: § 26-2-106(a): the maximum garnishable is '(1) Twenty-five percent (25%) of the disposable earnings for that week; or (2) The amount by which the disposable earnings for that week exceed thirty (30) times the federal minimum hourly wage ... whichever is less'; (b) equivalent amounts for other pay periods. § 26-2-107 (additional per-dependent-child exemption) was not read. Source is FindLaw's copy of the Tennessee Code, marked 'last updated January 02, 2024'; no primary text was reachable, so later amendments would not show.

tools_of_trade.notes: 'The debtor's aggregate interest, not to exceed one thousand nine hundred dollars ($1,900) in value in any implements, professional books, or tools of the trade of the debtor or the trade of a dependent of the debtor'. Source is FindLaw's copy of the Tennessee Code, marked 'last updated January 02, 2024'; no primary text was reachable, so later amendments would not show.

retirement.amount_text: Unlimited: IRC 401(a), 403(a), 403(b), 408 and 408A plans, Archer MSAs and HSAs, and state/local government pensions (except claims of the State and QDRO alternate payees)
retirement.notes: ERISA-qualified plans are excluded from the estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds regardless of state law. State cite: § 26-2-105(b) — funds or interests in retirement plans qualified under IRC §§ 401(a), 403(a), 403(b), 408 and 408A, Archer MSAs (§ 220) and HSAs (§ 223) 'are exempt from any and all claims of creditors of the participant or beneficiary, except the state'; (a) state and political-subdivision pensions; (c) QDRO alternate payees excepted. Read from FindLaw (secondary), last updated 1/2/2024.

texas.opt_out_statute: None — Texas has not enacted an opt-out under 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(2); Property Code chapters 41 and 42 contain no provision barring the federal § 522(d) exemptions, so debtors elect the federal set or the Texas set
texas.doubling_note: The personal-property cap is set per household status, not per debtor: $100,000 for property provided for a family versus $50,000 for a single adult who is not a member of a family (Prop. Code § 42.001(a)); the homestead is that 'of a family or a single, adult person' (§ 41.002). The statute does not give each spouse a separate $100,000.
texas.effective_date_note: No CPI indexing. § 42.001 dollar caps last amended by Acts 2007, 80th Leg., ch. 444 (H.B. 167), eff. 9/1/2007 (later 2015 amendment ch. 793 concerned religious books); § 41.002 acreage last amended by Acts 1999, 76th Leg., ch. 1510, eff. 1/1/2000. The session-law content of the 2007 act was not fetched; the effective dates come from the history notes on the official text.

homestead.amount_text: Unlimited value; urban homestead up to 10 acres; rural homestead up to 200 acres for a family or 100 acres for a single adult
homestead.statute: Tex. Prop. Code §§ 41.001, 41.002; Tex. Const. art. XVI, §§ 50-51
homestead.notes: § 41.001(a): 'A homestead and one or more lots used for a place of burial of the dead are exempt from seizure for the claims of creditors except for encumbrances properly fixed on homestead property' (purchase money, taxes, written improvement contracts, owelty, qualifying refinances, home-equity and reverse-mortgage liens). § 41.002: urban homestead (including one also used for a business) not more than 10 acres in one or more contiguous lots; rural homestead not more than 200 acres for a family or 100 acres for a single adult. § 41.001(c): sale proceeds protected for six months. No dollar cap appears in the statute. In bankruptcy, the federal 11 U.S.C. § 522(p) cap applies to homestead interest acquired within 1,215 days before filing (federal law, not read this pass).

motor_vehicle.amount_text: One motor vehicle for each family member or single adult who holds a driver's license (or relies on another to drive for them), within the $100,000 family / $50,000 single aggregate
motor_vehicle.notes: § 42.002(a)(9): 'a two-wheeled, three-wheeled, or four-wheeled motor vehicle for each member of a family or single adult who holds a driver's license or who does not hold a driver's license but who relies on another person to operate the vehicle for the benefit of the nonlicensed person'. Vehicles used in a trade are also covered by (a)(4). Counts toward the § 42.001(a) aggregate cap: $100,000 fair market value (exclusive of liens) for property provided for a family, $50,000 for a single adult who is not a member of a family.

household_goods.amount_text: $100,000 aggregate for a family / $50,000 for a single adult, covering home furnishings (incl. heirlooms), provisions, clothing, jewelry (capped at 25% of the aggregate), two firearms, sporting goods, vehicles, tools, listed livestock and pets
household_goods.notes: § 42.001(a): exempt if 'provided for a family and has an aggregate fair market value of not more than $100,000' or owned by a single adult not a member of a family and 'not more than $50,000', exclusive of liens. § 42.002(a) lists the eligible categories: (1) home furnishings including family heirlooms, (2) provisions, (3) farming or ranching vehicles and implements, (4) tools, equipment, books and apparatus including boats and motor vehicles used in a trade or profession, (5) wearing apparel, (6) jewelry up to 25% of the aggregate, (7) two firearms, (8) athletic and sporting equipment, (9) one vehicle per licensed family member, (10) two horses/mules/donkeys with tack, 12 cattle, 60 other livestock, 120 fowl and forage, (11) household pets. The single cap covers all of these together.

wildcard.amount_text: None (cash and bank accounts are not among the § 42.002 categories)
wildcard.notes: The § 42.001(a) aggregate applies only to the property categories listed in § 42.002(a); there is no any-property or cash category. Current wages (§ 42.001(b)(1)) and unpaid commissions (§ 42.001(d)) are separately protected.

wages.amount_text: Current wages for personal services fully exempt (except for court-ordered child support); unpaid commissions exempt up to 25% of the aggregate cap ($25,000 family / $12,500 single) and counted within it
wages.notes: § 42.001(b)(1): 'current wages for personal services, except for the enforcement of court-ordered child support payments' are exempt and not counted in the aggregate. (d): 'Unpaid commissions for personal services not to exceed 25 percent of the aggregate limitations prescribed by Subsection (a) are exempt from seizure and are included in the aggregate.'

tools_of_trade.amount_text: Tools, equipment, books and apparatus (including boats and motor vehicles) used in a trade or profession, plus farming/ranching vehicles and implements, within the $100,000 family / $50,000 single aggregate
tools_of_trade.notes: § 42.002(a)(3): farming or ranching vehicles and implements; (a)(4): 'tools, equipment, books, and apparatus, including boats and motor vehicles used in a trade or profession'. Counts toward the § 42.001(a) aggregate cap: $100,000 fair market value (exclusive of liens) for property provided for a family, $50,000 for a single adult who is not a member of a family.

retirement.amount_text: Unlimited: qualified savings plans (employer, government and church retirement plans, SEPs, IRAs and Roth IRAs including inherited ones, HSAs, Coverdell, Texas tuition plans, 529 and 529A accounts), in addition to the § 42.001 aggregate
retirement.notes: ERISA-qualified plans are excluded from the estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds regardless of state law. State cite: § 42.0021(b): 'In addition to the exemption prescribed by Section 42.001 and except as provided by this section, a person's interest in and right to receive payments from a qualified savings plan, whether vested or not, is exempt from attachment, execution, and seizure for the satisfaction of debts.' (a) defines qualified savings plans as tax-exempt or tax-deferred plans and lists 12 kinds, including inherited IRAs and Roth IRAs. The section's internal exceptions (subsections (c) onward) were not read in full this pass. Child-support liens are excepted by § 42.005 (except for education accounts).

texas.research_notes: All seven categories quoted from the official Property Code text. statutes.capitol.texas.gov is now a JavaScript single-page app that returns an empty shell to curl; its document files are served from tcss.legis.texas.gov/resources/PR/htm/PR.41.htm and PR.42.htm, which were downloaded and text-extracted locally. Opt-IN state: no opt-out provision exists, but no bankruptcy court page was fetched to confirm it. Texas's state set works differently from most: the homestead has no dollar cap (acreage only), and almost all personal property (furniture, vehicles, tools, jewelry, firearms, livestock) shares one $100,000 family / $50,000 single cap, so the vehicle, household-goods and tools rows all describe the same pool. There is no wildcard, so cash in the bank is unprotected under the state set; current wages are fully exempt. Federal § 522(p) limits recently acquired homestead equity in bankruptcy.

utah.doubling_note: Homestead: each joint owner is entitled to a homestead exemption but the per-household cap is twice the individual amount (78B-5-503(2)(b); 2026 caps $107,500 primary / $12,800 non-primary). homestead.amount_text: $53,700 primary personal residence (2026); $6,400 non-primary property; joint owners capped at $107,500 / $12,800 per household
homestead.notes: Statutory base amounts are $42,000 / $5,000 / $84,000 / $10,000 (May 2019 dollars); 78B-5-503(2)(e) directs the State Auditor to CPI-adjust them annually. The Auditor's January 2026 notice lists 2026 values: (2)(a)(i) $6,400; (2)(a)(ii) $53,700; (2)(b)(i) $12,800; (2)(b)(ii) $107,500. motor_vehicle.amount_text: $3,000 (one motor vehicle)
motor_vehicle.notes: Excludes vehicles designed or used primarily for recreation (OHVs, RVs) except a motorcycle or van used for daily transportation. A vehicle actually used in the debtor's trade may instead be claimed under the $5,000 tools-of-trade exemption in 78B-5-506(2) if no other exemption is applied to it. Not CPI-indexed (section last amended 2015).

household_goods.amount_text: $1,000 per category in each of 4 categories (sofas/chairs; dining and kitchen tables/chairs; animals, books, musical instruments; heirlooms/sentimental items) plus listed appliances, clothing, beds and 12 months' provisions without dollar limit
household_goods.notes: 78B-5-506(1) caps each of its four categories at $1,000 aggregate. 78B-5-505(1)(h) separately exempts, without a dollar cap, one washer, dryer, refrigerator, freezer, stove, microwave, sewing machine, all carpets in use, 12 months' provisions, all wearing apparel (not jewelry or furs) and all beds and bedding.

wildcard.amount_text: None
wildcard.notes: No general wildcard in the Utah Exemptions Act as currently codified. The introduced 2026 S.B. 112 proposed a $10,000 unused-homestead wildcard; the enrolled bill dropped it, and the current code text of 78B-5-505 contains no such provision.

secondary_claims.value: introduced version proposed a $10,000 unused-homestead wildcard; not enacted

wages.amount_text: Bankruptcy-specific: unpaid earnings due as of the petition date up to 1/24 of Utah median family income for the household size (paid more often than monthly) or 1/12 (paid monthly or less often), CPI-adjusted; general garnishment cap (Utah Code § 70C-7-103) not verified from a current primary source
wages.notes: 78B-5-505(1)(p) is a bankruptcy-only exemption of accrued unpaid earnings keyed to the Census Bureau's Utah state annual median family income for the debtor's household size, CPI-U adjusted. The general post-judgment garnishment limit in 70C-7-103 could only be fetched in a version marked 'Superseded 3/27/2014' (25% of disposable earnings or the amount above 30 x federal minimum wage); the current text was not retrievable, so that formula is not recorded as verified.

secondary_claims.value: 70C-7-103 (superseded 2014 text): lesser of 25% of disposable earnings or amount exceeding 30 x federal minimum hourly wage per week

tools_of_trade.amount_text: $5,000 (implements, professional books, tools of trade, including a motor vehicle with no other exemption applied)
tools_of_trade.notes: Must be actually used in the individual's principal business, trade, or profession.

retirement.amount_text: Unlimited (tax-qualified retirement plans and IRAs, including inherited accounts), except contributions made within one year before filing
retirement.notes: Covers plans described in IRC 401(a), 401(h), 401(k), 403(a), 403(b), 408, 408A, 409, 414(d), 414(e), 457, including inherited IRAs; does not apply to QDRO alternate payees or to amounts contributed within one year before the bankruptcy filing (except direct rollovers). ERISA-qualified plans are excluded from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds (401(k), 403(b), IRA, etc.) regardless of which state exemption scheme applies.

wildcard.notes: Bank accounts/cash have separate caps under (1)(d)(ii)-(iii) depending on debt type ($500 general / $2,000 consumer debt / $2,500 private student loan).

wages.amount_text: Greater of 80% of disposable earnings or 35 x state minimum hourly wage (consumer debt); greater of 75% or 35 x federal minimum wage (other debts); private student loans: greater of 85% or 50 x highest state minimum wage
wages.notes: RCW 6.15.050(1) makes the garnishment exemption claimable in bankruptcy to the same extent.

tools_of_trade.notes: Tools, instruments, materials and supplies used to carry on the debtor's trade.

retirement.amount_text: Unlimited (IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(a)/403(a)/403(b) plans, Keoghs, HSAs/MSAs, retirement bonds)
retirement.notes: Government plans are covered by their own statutes; child support and tax collection may reach benefits where federal law permits. ERISA-qualified plans are excluded from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds (401(k), 403(b), IRA, etc.) regardless of which state exemption scheme applies.

washington.research_notes: Washington has no opt-out statute; RCW 6.15.050(8) expressly contemplates a spouse exempting under 11 U.S.C. 522(d), and FindLaw (updated 8/3/2026) confirms the choice. Amounts rose in 2021-2025 (2021 c 50, 2023 c 393, 2025 c 391). The homestead is a formula, so a page should show '$125,000 or county median, whichever is greater' and point to the WCRER table rather than one number.

west-virginia.doubling_note: § 38-10-4 is framed as the debtor's interest per person and says nothing about joint filers; no primary source on doubling found.
west-virginia.effective_date_note: § 38-10-4 history shows amendments in 2021 (two sessions), 2022, 2023 and 2025; the session-law effective date of the most recent amendment was not shown on the page.

homestead.amount_text: $35,000 (residence or burial plot); $250,000 per household for physicians with $1M malpractice coverage in medical-liability cases
homestead.notes: Debtor's interest in real or personal property used as a residence by the debtor or a dependent, or a burial plot.

motor_vehicle.amount_text: $7,500 (one motor vehicle)

household_goods.amount_text: $16,000 aggregate, $800 per item (household furnishings, goods, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, musical instruments); jewelry $2,000 separately

wildcard.amount_text: $800 plus any unused portion of the $35,000 homestead exemption, in any property

wages.amount_text: 80% of wages (garnishment limited to 20%), and never below 50 x the federal minimum hourly wage per week
wages.notes: Suggestee execution may reach 20% of wages; payments may not reduce weekly take-home below 50 x the federal minimum hourly wage.

tools_of_trade.notes: Implements, professional books or tools of the trade of the debtor or a dependent.

retirement.amount_text: Pension/retirement plan payments exempt to the extent reasonably necessary for support (38-10-4(i)(5)); tax-exempt plans fully protected under federal law
retirement.notes: State text protects payments under a stock bonus, pension, profit-sharing, annuity or similar plan to the extent reasonably necessary for support of the debtor and dependents. ERISA-qualified plans are excluded from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds (401(k), 403(b), IRA, etc.) regardless of which state exemption scheme applies.

west-virginia.research_notes: West Virginia is no longer an opt-out state: § 38-10-4(k) states that solely for the purpose of applying 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(2) an individual debtor domiciled in this state may exempt the property specified under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d). Older secondary charts that call WV opt-out are wrong. The Southern District court page simply points to § 38-10-4. Effective date of the 2025 amendment not shown on the code page.

wisconsin.doubling_note: Homestead: § 815.20(1) says each spouse may claim a homestead exemption of not more than $75,000 in jointly owned or marital property. § 815.18 defines debtor as an individual and contains no joint-filer doubling language.
wisconsin.effective_date_note: docs.legis.wisconsin.gov shows § 815.18 current through 2025 Wis. Act 247 (through September 4, 2026); the year the current dollar amounts were set was not shown on the fetched text. No CPI indexing.

homestead.amount_text: $75,000 per owner ($150,000 for spouses)
homestead.notes: Each spouse may claim up to $75,000 in jointly owned/marital homestead property. No acreage limit stated.

motor_vehicle.amount_text: $4,000 aggregate, plus any unused consumer-goods exemption
motor_vehicle.notes: Unused amount of the $12,000 consumer-goods exemption under (3)(d) may be added.

household_goods.amount_text: $12,000 aggregate (consumer goods: household goods and furnishings, apparel, keepsakes, jewelry, etc.)

wildcard.amount_text: None
wildcard.notes: § 815.18(3) lists no any-property exemption; FindLaw likewise lists none. Depository accounts get their own $5,000 exemption under (3)(k).

secondary_claims.value: no wildcard listed

wages.amount_text: 75% of net income per one-week pay period, and not less than 30 x the greater of the state or federal minimum wage

tools_of_trade.amount_text: $15,000 aggregate (equipment, inventory, farm products, professional books used in the business)

retirement.amount_text: Unlimited (retirement, pension, disability and similar IRC-qualified plans, IRAs), with limits for owner-dominated plans
retirement.notes: ERISA-qualified plans are excluded from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. § 541(c)(2), and 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(C) exempts tax-exempt retirement funds (401(k), 403(b), IRA, etc.) regardless of which state exemption scheme applies.

wyoming.doubling_note: § 1-20-102(b): when two or more persons jointly own and occupy the same residence, each is entitled to the homestead exemption; § 1-20-106(a)(iii): each person occupying the same residence gets a separate household-goods exemption. Vehicle and tools exemptions are per person with no express joint rule.

wildcard.notes: No general any-property exemption appears in Title 1 ch. 20.
